paragraphs: The paper studies how to accelerate optimization when the object being updated is an entire probability distribution. It extends a variational formulation of accelerated optimization from vector variables to distributions. This shifts the question from how a point should move through a parameter space to how a distribution should evolve toward an objective.

The authors formulate this evolution as a mean-field optimal control problem. They construct a Lyapunov function to obtain a quantitative estimate of the asymptotic convergence rate. That result depends on the objective being displacement convex, so the stated theoretical guarantee concerns a particular class of objectives rather than arbitrary optimization over distributions.

For the important case where the objective is relative entropy, the paper provides two numerical approximations. These implement Hamilton’s equations through a collection of interacting particles, connecting the distribution-level formulation to computable algorithms. Numerical illustrations compare the resulting algorithm with MCMC and Hamiltonian MCMC. The abstract reports these comparisons without claiming a particular performance advantage over either method.
icml-2019-accelerated-flow-for-probabili.tldr: The paper develops accelerated optimization flows for probability distributions, with conditional convergence analysis and interacting-particle implementations.

paragraphs: A model used to choose between treatments needs to get the direction of the treatment effect right. This paper studies the reliability of such decisions when predictions come from observational data. A central concern is imbalance: treated and control groups can have different distributions of characteristics, which increases an upper bound on expected individual treatment-effect estimation error.

The proposed reliability measure estimates the model’s Type S error rate: the probability of predicting the wrong sign for a treatment effect. This connects uncertainty directly to a consequential decision error. A prediction that favors the wrong action matters differently from an inaccurate estimate that still favors the appropriate action.

The authors then use estimated reliability to guide active learning. When predictions are unreliable, the method can seek additional, potentially expensive observations instead of forcing an immediate choice. They demonstrate effectiveness on simulated binary-outcome data and a medical dataset with synthetic continuous treatment outcomes. These results support collecting information according to decision reliability in the studied settings.
icml-2019-active-learning-for-decision-m.tldr: The method guides data collection using the estimated probability that a treatment-effect model recommends the wrong direction of action.

paragraphs: Using BERT for several language-understanding tasks can require keeping a separate fine-tuned model for each task. Although these models begin from the same pretrained model, their parameters are stored separately. This paper investigates whether a single shared BERT model can serve multiple tasks while retaining enough task-specific flexibility to perform well.

The authors introduce projected attention layers, or PALs, as adaptation modules. These add a small number of parameters specific to each task while allowing the main BERT model to be shared. The approach makes multi-task learning a way to reuse model capacity across related tasks, with dedicated additions providing adaptation for individual tasks.

On the GLUE benchmark, the resulting system matches the performance of separately fine-tuned models while using approximately seven times fewer parameters. It also achieves a reported state-of-the-art result on Recognizing Textual Entailment. The parameter comparison concerns serving the collection of tasks, illustrating how shared modeling can reduce the total capacity needed without sacrificing the reported benchmark performance.
icml-2019-bert-and-pals-projected-attent.tldr: PALs let one shared BERT model match separately fine-tuned models on GLUE with approximately seven times fewer parameters.

paragraphs: Evaluating a new decision policy from logged contextual bandit feedback requires estimating what would have happened under different choices. This counterfactual problem arises in both offline A/B testing and learning a policy from existing records. The paper develops a family of estimators that encompasses most previously proposed approaches and uses its analysis to identify Continuous Adaptive Blending, or CAB.

CAB addresses the balance between systematic estimation error and variability. The authors show that it can have substantially less bias than clipped inverse propensity weighting and the Direct Method. It can also have lower variance than Doubly Robust and inverse propensity estimators. These are possible advantages established by the analysis, rather than a claim that CAB dominates every alternative in every setting.

CAB is also sub-differentiable, allowing it to participate in optimization for policy learning, unlike the SWITCH estimator discussed in the paper. Experiments report strong evaluation accuracy and better learning performance than the other counterfactual estimators tested. Its contribution therefore covers both assessing policies and using those assessments to improve them.
icml-2019-cab-continuous-adaptive-blendi.tldr: CAB provides a counterfactual estimator that can improve bias and variance trade-offs while supporting policy learning.

paragraphs: Training memory includes more than the model’s parameters. Many gradient optimizers maintain auxiliary variables whose storage grows with model size. This paper targets that additional memory by representing optimizer state through a compressed linear sketch, allowing the optimization method to retain useful information in less space.

The theoretical analysis shows that count-sketch optimization preserves the convergence rate of stochastic gradient descent. Evaluations include ResNet-18 and Transformer-XL. On the 1-Billion Word dataset, the authors report training memory of 7.7 GB instead of 10.8 GB, described as a 25% saving, with minimal accuracy and performance loss. This gives an empirical example of reducing memory while largely preserving training behavior.

The saved memory can also change how training is run. On an Amazon extreme classification task with more than 49.5 million classes, it allows a 3.5-fold increase in mini-batch size and accompanies a 38% reduction in training time. That result connects optimizer-state compression to throughput: its value can extend beyond fitting a model into memory.
icml-2019-compressing-gradient-optimizer.tldr: Count-sketch compression reduces optimizer-state memory while preserving an SGD convergence rate and enabling practical training savings.

paragraphs: A learning system that stores past experiences also needs a practical way to retrieve useful memories as its store grows. The Contextual Memory Tree addresses this problem with a learned memory controller. It works online, inserting new memories into an experience store whose size is not fixed in advance.

The tree supports insertion and retrieval in logarithmic time. This makes it suitable as an added memory component for existing statistical learning algorithms without substantially increasing their training and inference computation. Its learning problem is expressed as a reduction to classification, allowing improvements in classification representations or architectures to benefit the memory controller as well.

The authors augment multi-class and multi-label classification algorithms with this memory and observe statistical improvements. They also evaluate it on image-captioning tasks, where it performs better computationally than a simple nearest-neighbor memory system and benefits from reward learning. The findings connect efficient memory access with learned retrieval behavior, showing that the store can contribute to predictions while remaining computationally manageable.
icml-2019-contextual-memory-trees-90bd81.tldr: Contextual Memory Trees add learned, growing experience stores to models with logarithmic-time insertion and retrieval.

paragraphs: A regression model can predict a distribution over possible target values, giving a description of uncertainty alongside its prediction. For that description to be useful, the distribution must be well calibrated. This paper focuses on improving the reliability of these uncertainty outputs and introduces a concept called distribution calibration.

The authors demonstrate advantages of distribution calibration over an existing notion based on quantiles. This changes the object of evaluation: the goal is to assess calibration at the level of the predicted distribution, while also considering quantile-level behavior. The distinction matters because the paper treats distribution calibration as a separate target for making regression uncertainty more trustworthy.

To improve predictions, the authors propose a post-hoc method built from multi-output Gaussian processes and a new Beta link function. It operates on previously trained regression models, making calibration an additional adjustment to their outputs. Experiments across common regression models show improvements in both distribution-level and quantile-level calibration, supporting the method as a practical way to refine predicted uncertainty.
icml-2019-distribution-calibration-for-r.tldr: The paper introduces distribution calibration and a post-hoc Gaussian-process method that improves regression uncertainty calibration.

paragraphs: Large matrix multiplications can be divided into smaller tasks and distributed across computing nodes. Some nodes finish slowly, so coding methods make it possible to recover the desired result without waiting for every task. The paper addresses how to organize such coded work when the matrices are split across three dimensions.

The authors introduce dual entangled polynomial codes, or DEP codes. Compared with entangled polynomial codes, their construction requires around 25% fewer tasks for decoding. Each DEP task performs two matrix multiplications, making the amount of work within a task an essential part of interpreting that reduction. The result concerns the required task count, rather than an equivalent percentage reduction in all computation.

Experiments in a real cloud environment show that DEP codes can also reduce decoding overhead and memory consumption within tasks. These findings give the construction practical relevance beyond its task-count advantage. The paper advances three-dimensional coding for large distributed products without claiming in the abstract to achieve the optimal possible decoding threshold.
icml-2019-dual-entangled-polynomial-code.tldr: DEP codes require around 25% fewer decoding tasks than EP codes by assigning two matrix multiplications to each task.

paragraphs: When more computing resources become available, a convolutional network can be made deeper, wider, or given higher-resolution inputs. This paper studies how those choices interact and finds that carefully balancing them can improve performance. Its compound scaling method uses a single coefficient to coordinate growth across all three dimensions.

The authors demonstrate the scaling approach on MobileNets and ResNet. They then use neural architecture search to create a baseline network and scale it into the EfficientNet family. This combines a chosen starting architecture with a systematic rule for increasing capacity, making scaling itself a central part of the model design.

EfficientNet-B7 reaches 84.4% top-1 and 97.1% top-5 ImageNet accuracy, with reported size and inference-speed advantages of 8.4-fold and 6.1-fold over the compared best existing ConvNet. The family also transfers well, achieving reported state-of-the-art accuracy on five transfer datasets with an order of magnitude fewer parameters. These results support balanced scaling as a route to improved accuracy and efficiency together.
icml-2019-efficientnet-rethinking-model-.tldr: EfficientNet improves convolutional-network accuracy and efficiency by coordinating the scaling of depth, width, and input resolution.

paragraphs: When a domain has known transformation rules, a network architecture can incorporate that knowledge. This paper introduces Equivariant Transformers, differentiable mappings from images to images that improve robustness to predefined continuous transformation groups. The approach makes those specified transformations part of the model’s construction.

The key mechanism is a specially derived canonical coordinate system. Within these coordinates, the model includes functions whose responses respect the transformations by construction. The authors also show empirically that multiple Equivariant Transformers can be composed to improve robustness to more complicated transformation groups involving several parameters. This connects the basic construction to settings with multiple transformation dimensions.

On a real-world image-classification task, adding these components improves the sample efficiency of ResNet classifiers. In the limited-data setting, the reported relative reduction in error reaches up to 15%, while the parameter count increases by less than 1%. The result indicates that encoding relevant transformation knowledge can help a model learn effectively from fewer examples with a small parameter increase.
icml-2019-equivariant-transformer-networ.tldr: Equivariant Transformers encode predefined image transformations into network structure and improve limited-data classification with few additional parameters.

paragraphs: Adaptive optimizers such as Adam and RMSProp are widely used, but explaining their behavior in nonconvex optimization is difficult. This paper views adaptive methods as stochastic gradient descent equipped with a preconditioner: a transformation that changes how gradient updates are scaled. The preconditioner is estimated online as optimization proceeds.

Studying that transformation separately reveals a proposed reason for its effectiveness. Near stationary points, it rescales stochastic gradient noise so that the noise is isotropic, without a preferred direction. The analysis shows how this property helps the optimizer escape saddle points. The authors also establish that adaptive methods can efficiently estimate the relevant preconditioner.

Combining these pieces yields a second-order convergence result for an adaptive method, described by the authors as the first such result to their knowledge. Their analysis indicates faster escape from saddle points than SGD and the possibility of faster overall convergence to second-order stationary points. This supplies a specific theoretical mechanism for adaptive optimization benefits rather than a universal speed guarantee for every use of Adam or RMSProp.
icml-2019-escaping-saddle-points-with-ad.tldr: The analysis explains how adaptive gradient scaling can reshape noise to escape saddle points faster and improve second-order convergence.

paragraphs: Attend-Infer-Repeat models a visual scene as a composition of individual objects and learns this structure without supervision through Bayesian inference. Its object appearances are represented with variational autoencoders. The paper identifies difficult inference in the overall model as an obstacle that slows learning and makes suboptimal solutions more likely.

The proposed replacement, SuPAIR, uses sum-product networks to represent objects. These are expressive probabilistic models that support tractable inference routines. Changing the object representation therefore changes the computational burden of reasoning about the scene, while retaining the goal of understanding an image through its constituent objects.

The resulting model is reported to learn an order of magnitude faster than AIR. It also handles object occlusions consistently and permits a background noise model, improving robustness in Bayesian scene understanding. These contributions address both learning efficiency and the treatment of imperfect visual evidence. The paper’s central finding is that choosing tractable object-level probability models can substantially improve the behavior of a structured scene model.
icml-2019-faster-attend-infer-repeat-wit.tldr: SuPAIR replaces AIR’s object representations with sum-product networks, yielding an order-of-magnitude learning speedup and improved robustness.

paragraphs: Variational autoencoders learn probability models through a generative model and an inference network that must work together. Their interaction can make learning and inference difficult, especially in high dimensions. This paper addresses that difficulty by decomposing the overall modeling problem into smaller, lower-dimensional pieces.

The proposed architecture is a hierarchical mixture of VAE experts. Each expert handles a smaller problem, and a sum-product network represents the hierarchy that coordinates them. This makes decomposition part of the probability model itself: the experts contribute within an organized mixture rather than being treated as unrelated models.

In experiments, the hierarchical models outperform classical VAEs on almost all of the evaluated benchmarks. The authors also report strong data efficiency and a gradual decline in performance when training data becomes extremely scarce. Together, these results support the usefulness of coordinating smaller VAE problems, particularly when high-dimensional learning or limited data makes a single VAE difficult to train effectively. The empirical claim retains exceptions among the tested benchmarks.
icml-2019-hierarchical-decompositional-m.tldr: A sum-product hierarchy coordinates low-dimensional VAE experts, improving most tested benchmarks and remaining effective with very little data.

paragraphs: Representing a directed acyclic graph with continuous embeddings becomes difficult when both ancestor and descendant relationships grow exponentially. The paper targets this structural challenge, which extends beyond the simpler setting of trees. Its goal is to give complex directed relationships a suitable geometric representation.

The authors introduce Disk Embeddings, a framework that embeds these graphs into quasi-metric spaces. They show that Order Embeddings and Hyperbolic Entailment Cones fit within this framework through Euclidean space and spheres, respectively. This provides a common formulation for methods that otherwise appear to use different geometric constructions.

Within that framework, the paper proposes Hyperbolic Disk Embeddings specifically to handle exponential growth in relationships. Experiments show that the Disk Embedding models outperform existing methods, with particularly strong results on complex graphs that are not trees. The findings support matching the embedding geometry to the graph’s relational structure. The contribution includes both a unifying perspective on earlier methods and a new construction aimed at harder graph structures.
icml-2019-hyperbolic-disk-embeddings-for.tldr: Disk Embeddings unify existing graph embeddings and introduce a hyperbolic construction that performs especially well on complex directed acyclic graphs.

paragraphs: The Insertion Transformer generates a sequence by repeatedly inserting tokens wherever they belong in the current output. It can therefore use generation orders beyond the usual left-to-right sequence. This changes decoding from extending one endpoint to developing multiple parts of an output over successive iterations.

Training can encourage a particular order, including left-to-right generation or a binary-tree traversal. It can also maximize entropy across valid insertions to encourage robustness. At decoding time, the same framework accommodates one insertion at a time or simultaneous insertions at several locations, allowing different degrees of parallel generation.

The authors evaluate these choices on WMT 2014 English-German translation. They report better performance than many earlier non-autoregressive translation approaches at comparable or greater parallelism. The model also recovers the original Transformer’s performance while requiring only logarithmically many decoding iterations. The result shows that flexibility in generation order can support efficient parallel decoding while retaining strong translation quality in the evaluated task.
icml-2019-insertion-transformer-flexible.tldr: The Insertion Transformer generates tokens at multiple positions, matching original Transformer translation performance with logarithmically many decoding iterations.

paragraphs: Comparing sequences of multidimensional vectors requires accounting for their structure and the dependence among their elements. The paper focuses on the ground metric, the rule used to compare individual vectors within those sequences. Because this rule influences the overall sequence distance, learning it offers a way to improve sequence comparisons.

The method learns a Mahalanobis ground metric from labeled sequences. It assumes that the way vector-level comparisons induce the full sequence distance is given. Its objective encourages sequences from the same class to have small distances and sequences from different classes to have large distances, linking the learned metric to the desired discrimination.

To reduce the number of constraints, the authors associate each sequence with a virtual sequence and bring the pair closer under the chosen distance. They develop an iterative solution applicable to sequence distances based on a ground metric. Experiments on several sequence datasets demonstrate effectiveness and efficiency, supporting adaptation of the underlying vector comparison as a general strategy for learning structured sequence distances.
icml-2019-learning-distance-for-sequence.tldr: The method learns sequence distances by adapting a Mahalanobis metric for their component vectors and reducing optimization constraints with virtual sequences.

paragraphs: Regularization aims to improve how a learned model performs beyond its training data, but choosing its strength or other hyperparameters can be difficult. This paper approaches that choice through the generalization gap. It views regularizers as upper bounds on that gap and seeks to reduce the extra slack in those bounds.

For a broad class of regularizers, the hyperparameters producing the best upper bound can be found with linear programming. This turns the bound-based selection problem into a structured optimization task. Tightening the bound can improve test performance, providing the motivation for using this calculation to guide regularization.

Under certain Bayesian assumptions, solving the linear program allows a direct move to optimal hyperparameters using very limited data. That conditional result motivates a practical tuning algorithm, whose effectiveness is demonstrated on real and synthetic datasets. The distinction matters: the optimality claim relies on the stated assumptions, while the experiments support the usefulness of the resulting tuning approach in the evaluated settings.
icml-2019-learning-optimal-linear-regula.tldr: The paper tunes regularizers through linear-programming bounds on generalization, with direct optimal selection under certain Bayesian assumptions.

paragraphs: A controller’s action frequency changes the time interval between decisions, even when the underlying environment is nearly continuous. This paper identifies that discretization choice as an important source of instability in deep reinforcement learning. Changes in frames per second or control frequency can therefore affect learning behavior in consequential ways.

The authors empirically find that Q-learning approaches, including Deep Q-learning and Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient, collapse as time steps become small. They also provide a formal result that Q-learning does not exist in continuous time. This gives a theoretical basis for examining sensitivity to increasingly fine decision intervals.

The paper then develops a principled off-policy reinforcement-learning algorithm designed to maintain similar performance across a broad range of time discretizations. Experiments confirm the claimed robustness across the tested intervals. Its contribution is to treat time resolution as a structural algorithm-design issue and provide an approach that is less sensitive to this particular environmental choice, rather than claiming to resolve every source of deep reinforcement-learning instability.
icml-2019-making-deep-q-learning-methods.tldr: The paper explains Q-learning’s failure at small time steps and develops an off-policy approach robust across many time discretizations.

paragraphs: The paper studies several Mallows models for ranking data, with attention to both statistical estimation and model structure. One part examines the statistical properties of the maximum likelihood estimator for Mallows’ phi model. This investigates the behavior of fitting the model to observed rankings, complementing the paper’s algorithmic contribution.

The authors also connect different Mallows ranking models using recent mathematical developments. Their model-selection problem is motivated by an infinite top-t ranking model, where t determines the model size. Choosing this value automatically makes the amount of ranking structure included in the model part of the learning procedure.

The proposed selection algorithm uses the renewal property of an infinite random permutation as its central idea. This links a mathematical property of the ranking process to a concrete procedure for choosing t. The algorithm performs well on several datasets. The contribution combines analysis of an established estimator, connections among ranking models, and an empirically supported method for automatic model-size selection.
icml-2019-mallows-ranking-models-maximum.tldr: The paper analyzes Mallows ranking estimators and uses a renewal property to select ranking-model size automatically.

paragraphs: MASS develops pretraining specifically for encoder-decoder language generation. It hides a randomly selected consecutive fragment of a sentence, gives the remaining sentence to an encoder, and trains a decoder to reconstruct the missing fragment. The task connects understanding available text with generating the portion that has been removed.

Because reconstruction uses both components, the pretraining jointly develops the encoder’s representation extraction and the decoder’s language modeling. The pretrained system is then fine-tuned for generation tasks with little or no task-specific training resources. This makes the pretraining objective relevant to the coordinated work an encoder and decoder must perform downstream.

Across translation, summarization, and conversational response generation on eight datasets, MASS significantly improves over the tested baselines without pretraining or with other pretraining methods. For unsupervised English-French translation, the authors report 30.02 BLEU and a state-of-the-art result, exceeding an early attention-based supervised model. These findings support fragment reconstruction as useful preparation for the evaluated low- and zero-resource generation tasks.
icml-2019-mass-masked-sequence-to-sequen.tldr: MASS jointly pretrains an encoder and decoder by reconstructing masked sentence fragments, improving low- and zero-resource language generation.

paragraphs: Learning from an expert is harder when demonstrations show observations but omit the actions that produced them. This paper studies that setting in large-scale Markov decision processes. It introduces Forward Adversarial Imitation Learning, or FAIL, a model-free algorithm that learns from the expert’s observation sequences.

FAIL learns a sequence of policies that can differ across time. Its objective minimizes an Integral Probability Metric between the observation distributions produced by the learner and the expert. This gives the learner a distribution-level target even though the demonstrations do not directly specify which actions to imitate.

The authors prove that FAIL learns a near-optimal policy with a sample requirement polynomial in the relevant parameters and independent of the number of distinct observations. The result extends provable sample efficiency beyond earlier work typically restricted to tabular settings or access to a near-optimal reset distribution. Experiments on several OpenAI Gym control tasks also demonstrate effectiveness, linking the theoretical approach to practical control evaluations.
icml-2019-provably-efficient-imitation-l.tldr: FAIL learns from expert observations without action labels and provides a near-optimality guarantee with sample complexity independent of observation count.

paragraphs: In cooperative multi-agent learning, agents can train with shared information but must later choose actions independently. Value factorization connects those stages by expressing a joint action-value function through individual ones. The paper argues that the additive structure of VDN and the monotonic structure of QMIX restrict which factorizable tasks those methods can represent.

QTRAN takes a different route: it transforms the original joint action-value function into one that is easier to factorize while preserving the optimal actions. This makes the transformation itself central to coordinating decentralized decisions. The authors guarantee a more general factorization than VDN or QMIX, covering a wider class of tasks without their particular structural restrictions.

Experiments on multi-domain Gaussian-squeeze and modified predator-prey tasks show superior performance for QTRAN. The margins are especially large when payoffs penalize non-cooperative behavior more aggressively. This finding connects the broader representation to situations where coordination strongly affects reward, while the theoretical claim remains about a wider class of factorizable tasks rather than every possible multi-agent problem.
icml-2019-qtran-learning-to-factorize-wi.tldr: QTRAN transforms joint action values while preserving optimal actions, enabling more general decentralized value factorization than VDN or QMIX.

paragraphs: Using softmax in reinforcement-learning value updates raises theoretical concerns: it can produce suboptimal values and disrupt the Bellman operator’s contraction properties. Yet this paper reports that combining the softmax Bellman operator with Deep Q-learning produces better policies in practice, even outperforming a double Q-learning counterpart. The observed benefit is independent of softmax’s role in exploration.

The authors prove that the softmax operator approaches the standard Bellman operator exponentially quickly as the inverse temperature parameter increases. They also bound the distance between its Q-function and the optimal Q-function. These results characterize approximation behavior, but the authors explicitly recognize that they do not by themselves explain the stronger practical policies.

A further analysis shows that softmax can reduce overestimation error. This offers a possible explanation for why an operator with suboptimal theoretical values can help when value functions are approximated. The paper compares different Bellman operators to expose their trade-offs, framing operator selection as a balance among properties rather than an automatic preference for a single update rule.
icml-2019-revisiting-the-softmax-bellman.tldr: The softmax Bellman operator can improve Deep Q-learning policies, with reduced overestimation offering a possible explanation despite theoretical drawbacks.

paragraphs: Disentangled representations aim to separate underlying sources of variation in complex data. Such separation matters for data efficiency and robustness, but evaluating whether a representation achieves it requires a clear definition. This paper addresses the absence of a commonly accepted definition and validation procedure through a causal perspective on representation learning.

The proposed framework includes disentanglement and robustness to domain shifts as special cases. Bringing them into a common causal formulation supports a new metric for evaluating deep latent-variable models quantitatively. The contribution focuses on making representation quality assessable through that framework, giving a concrete evaluation target to an otherwise broad modeling objective.

The authors show how to estimate the metric from labeled observational data and provide an efficient algorithm whose cost grows linearly with dataset size. This makes the proposed evaluation usable without requiring the estimation procedure to scale superlinearly with the number of examples. Together, the causal formulation and estimator connect a conceptual account of robust representations to a practical validation method.
icml-2019-robustly-disentangled-causal-m.tldr: A causal framework unifies disentanglement and domain-shift robustness and yields a metric estimable from labeled observational data in linear time.

paragraphs: Deep neural networks can memorize training examples even when their labels are highly unreliable. This makes noisy labels a source of overfitting: fitting the supplied answers can reinforce mistakes in the data. SELFIE addresses the problem through a training method that selectively corrects and reuses unclean examples.

Its central idea is to refurbish samples whose labels can be corrected with high precision. As those examples become usable, the available training set grows gradually. Selectivity matters because mistaken corrections can introduce further noise; the method’s design aims to prevent that accumulation while making fuller use of the training data.

The authors evaluate SELFIE on four real-world or synthetic datasets and report substantial improvements in absolute test error compared with two state-of-the-art methods. These findings support the usefulness of recovering selected noisy examples during training. The contribution combines label correction with careful sample reuse, treating the reliability of a correction as important to whether an example should contribute to learning.
icml-2019-selfie-refurbishing-unclean-sa.tldr: SELFIE selectively corrects and reuses noisy-label examples, expanding usable training data and reducing test error in the reported experiments.
